name: Cinoxate
lead: Cinoxate is an organic UVB filter, an ester of methoxycinnamic acid and 2-ethoxyethanol, used in some sunscreen formulations [1]. Sunscreen filters help appearance indirectly: by absorbing sunburn-producing ultraviolet light before it damages skin, they reduce burning and the cumulative photoaging, such as wrinkles, dark spots and sagging, that shows up in how skin looks over time [5].

According to Wikipedia, the US FDA approved cinoxate as a UV filter in 1961, and a 2023 review cited there describes it as no longer commonly used in cosmetic formulations [1]. It belongs to the methoxycinnamate family alongside octyl methoxycinnamate (octinoxate) and amiloxate [1][4].

Published research on cinoxate is sparse. A 1989 laboratory study found it increased chromosome-level changes in cultured hamster cells exposed to certain damaging agents, and a 2024 computational and cell study flagged it as a PPAR-gamma agonist; neither involved human use [2][3].

paras: Cinoxate, also called 2-ethoxyethyl p-methoxycinnamate, has the formula C14H18O4 and a molar mass of about 250 g/mol. It is a slightly yellow, viscous liquid that is insoluble in water but mixes with alcohols, esters and vegetable oils [1]. It belongs to the cinnamate family, a group of derivatives widely used in cosmetics for functions including perfuming and UV absorption [4].

Cinnamic acid derivatives used as UV filters include octinoxate, amiloxate, octocrylene and cinoxate. A 2018 review notes that their maximum concentrations in cosmetics are restricted because of adverse effects such as contact and photocontact allergy [4]. Researchers have also described an enzymatic route to synthesising cinoxate in aqueous conditions, as a demonstration of green esterification [6].

Organic (chemical) sunscreen filters absorb ultraviolet radiation and release the energy as heat, in contrast with mineral filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide [5]. Cinoxate is classified as a UVB filter [1]. Sun protection factor (SPF) expresses the fraction of sunburn-producing radiation that reaches the skin, so SPF 15 means about one-fifteenth gets through under standard application [5].

Cinoxate has been used as a UVB filter in sunscreens and is grouped with other cinnamates such as octyl methoxycinnamate [1]. The FDA approved it in 1961, and a 2023 review described it as not commonly used in cosmetics now [1]. Wikipedia's sunscreen article lists it among filters approved in some jurisdictions, including Australia and Canada [5]. It also appears in older patent and formulation literature, including a 1990 liquid detergent containing sunscreen agents and a 1977 study of sunscreen agents protecting dyed tablet coatings from fading [7][8].

Regulation of sunscreen ingredients differs by region. In the United States sunscreen is classed as an over-the-counter drug, which has slowed approval of new filters, and in 2021 the FDA sorted filters into categories, listing only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide as generally recognised as safe and effective [5]. In the European Union sunscreens are cosmetics under Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 [5].

A 2013 Australian study of roughly 900 people, summarised on Wikipedia, found that daily broad-spectrum sunscreen over four and a half years produced smoother, more resilient skin than usual practice, and another study of 32 subjects reported reversal of photoaging within 12 weeks of daily SPF 30 use [5]. These studies concern sunscreens as products and did not isolate cinoxate.

In a 1989 study, cinoxate enhanced sister-chromatid exchanges and chromosome aberrations induced by mitomycin C, 4-nitroquinoline-1-oxide or UV light in cultured Chinese hamster ovary cells. The authors suggested the compounds inhibit DNA excision repair [2]. A 2024 cheminformatic analysis of 8,435 Tox21 compounds identified methoxycinnamate UV filters as enriched for PPAR-gamma agonist activity; experimentally, cinoxate bound PPAR-gamma (Ki 18.0 micromolar) and elicited an obesogenic phenotype in human bone marrow stem cells during adipogenic differentiation [3]. These are laboratory findings, and the authors framed them as needing further testing.
No studies found of cinoxate in human trials. Related research is limited to cell-culture and computational work [2][3] and to broader reviews of cinnamate derivatives in cosmetics [4].

card.summary: An older cinnamate UVB filter, approved in the US in 1961 and now rarely used.
card.note: Little modern research; only cell-culture and computational safety findings exist.

quick.overview:
Cinoxate is a cinnamate-based UVB filter that the US FDA approved in 1961. It appeared in some older sunscreens.

A 2023 review cited by Wikipedia describes it as no longer commonly used in cosmetics.
quick.mechanism: As a cinnamate ester, it absorbs ultraviolet B light in the skin's surface layers.
quick.risks: No human safety trials are documented in the sources. A 1989 cell study reported increased chromosome changes when combined with other agents, and a 2024 computational study predicted PPAR-gamma activity.

chain: Cinoxate absorbs UVB light in a sunscreen
Less UVB reaches the skin, so less burning and cumulative photodamage
Skin keeps a smoother, more even appearance with age
angle.text: As a UVB-absorbing ingredient, cinoxate contributes to the sun protection of a sunscreen. Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen use is associated in studies with smoother, more resilient skin and slower visible photoaging, though those studies concern sunscreens generally, not cinoxate specifically.
